_comment: The slope standard Dozer Country paints by. Everything here is data on purpose:
a colored overlay that says 'you can cut here' is a safety claim, and a safety
claim has to be auditable by the person whose ground it is. Nothing here is
compiled into the plugin: read it, check it against the tables, and if a number
is wrong say so. Changing it takes a rebuild -- the plugin deliberately reads
ONLY this asset from inside its own signed APK, and never an override from
shared storage, because a colour table that decides where a dozer can work must
not be editable by anything else on the phone.
Two different things live in each standard, and they are NOT the same axis:
bands  - production classes. Slope MAGNITUDE only. From the NWCG production
rate tables, which are measured for line built UP or DOWN the slope
and have no sideslope column at all.
limits - safety refusal points, DIRECTIONAL. From the S-232 Dozer Boss course.
A 50% slope is production class 3 and at the same time over the 45%
sidehill limit. Which one applies depends on the way the line runs.
The AOI overlay knows magnitude only, so it paints bands. The line profile knows
direction, so it can also check limits.
To add a second standard (e.g. CAL FIRE), append another object to 'standards'.
The plugin shows a picker as soon as there is more than one.

workingWindow.label: one chain (66 ft)
_comment: A patch of good ground smaller than this is not called workable. A single
cell at 20% inside a 60% face is not dozer country, so each cell is
classified by the WORST slope within this distance of it.
One chain is the unit the production tables already count in (chains per
hour), and it is about the limit of what 30 m DTED2 posts can honestly
resolve. Anything smaller is made up.
Water is left unpainted rather than classed. There is no hydrography in ATAK
for a plugin to ask -- not one water, coastline or bathymetry class in
main.jar -- so water is found in the elevation itself: a connected run of
cells all holding PRECISELY the same value, covering at least this area.
Real terrain always varies, even at DTED's one metre quantisation. A water
surface is rendered dead flat because that is what it is. The ocean is one
enormous such region at zero; a reservoir is a smaller one at its own level,
which is why this finds lakes as well as sea without knowing where sea level
is.
It is NOT the same as 'low slope'. Low slope would swallow the Oxnard plain,
which is exactly the good dozer ground this overlay exists to find.
What it gets wrong: a dry lake bed is dead flat too and will be masked, which
removes genuinely workable ground. The pane reports how much was masked so
that is visible rather than silent. Raise this number if it is over-masking
ground you know; set it to 0 to turn the mask off entirely.

standards.name: NWCG
sources: NWCG Fire Line Production Rate Tables (2021), table 'Dozer Fireline Construction Rates (Single Pass) in Chains per Hour', carried forward from the Fireline Handbook PMS 410-1. Public domain.
USFS/NWCG S-232 Dozer Boss, Pre-Course Work, Appendix D, for the directional limits.

Off the table for most of the book

aboveStandard.label: Over 74%
aboveStandard.meaning: Past where the standard goes at all
aboveStandard._comment: The production table stops at 74%. This is not 'very steep class 4' -- it is unmeasured ground, and it is colored so it does not read as a band.

_comment: S-232 Dozer Boss, Appendix D, verbatim: 'As with any piece of specialized
equipment, the dozer has limitations. As a general guideline, dozers should
not be operated across slopes (sidehill) greater than 45 percent, uphill
slopes greater than 55 percent or downhill on slopes greater than 75
percent.'
Corroborated by the S-232 supplement 'Mechanized Equipment for Fire and
Fuels Operations': 'According to the Fireline Handbook, dozers are limited
to <75% favorable slopes.'
These are GENERAL GUIDELINES. Type and size of dozer, terrain, weather and
operator experience all move them, and the standard says so.
